security_audit.summary: The audit reviewed 80 static findings; 79 are documentation-related false positives. One finding is confirmed because an example imports an OpenAPI specification from a mutable branch. Semantic review also found caller-controlled rate-limit keys and commands that expose subscription keys.

remediation.issue: Rate limits use an unverified request header as the caller identity.
remediation.suggestion: Derive counters from authenticated subscriptions or validated token claims, and test that changing headers cannot reset limits.

remediation.issue: Examples print active APIM subscription keys into agent-visible command output.
remediation.suggestion: Prefer managed identity, retrieve unavoidable keys outside model context, and redact secrets from terminals, prompts, traces, and logs.

remediation.issue: An API import reads an OpenAPI specification from a mutable GitHub branch.
remediation.suggestion: Pin the specification to a reviewed commit and verify its digest before importing it into APIM.

semantic_findings.title: Caller-Controlled Rate-Limit Key
semantic_findings.description: Examples use the unverified X-Agent-Id request header as an APIM rate-limit counter key. Callers can rotate values to evade limits.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: Both examples directly trust a caller-supplied header without authentication or validation. Rotating that value creates a clear rate-limit bypass.

semantic_findings.title: Subscription Keys Exposed to Agent Output
semantic_findings.description: Commands retrieve APIM subscription keys and a primary tracing key as terminal output. Agent sessions and logs could retain these active secrets.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The commands explicitly request subscription key material, including primaryKey, and print it for subsequent use. This exposes credentials to the invoking agent context.

content.value_statement: AI teams need consistent controls for models, tools, and agents. This skill guides Azure API Management configuration for security, cost control, routing, and diagnostics.
actual_capabilities: Configure APIM backends for Azure OpenAI and AI Foundry endpoints.
Apply token limits, semantic caching, token metrics, and content safety policies.
Set up managed identity authentication and Azure RBAC for backend access.
Configure backend pools, retries, streaming support, and multi-tenant controls.
Diagnose authentication, quota, cache, safety, backend, and health-check failures.
limitations: Requires Azure CLI and existing Azure resources; it does not deploy APIM.
Examples use placeholders and must be reviewed before execution.
Some APIM AI policies and backend pools depend on service tier, region, or preview availability.
Streaming does not support semantic caching or token metrics in the documented patterns.

use_cases.title: Govern Shared Model Access
use_cases.description: Create centralized APIM controls for token budgets, caching, routing, and metrics across multiple AI applications.

use_cases.title: Protect Agent Tools
use_cases.description: Add authentication, content safety, and authenticated rate limits to APIs exposed as MCP tools.

use_cases.title: Review Gateway Controls
use_cases.description: Evaluate managed identity, RBAC, tenant isolation, content filtering, and operational diagnostics before production rollout.

prompt_templates.title: Inspect an Existing Gateway
prompt_templates.prompt: Inspect APIM instance <name> in resource group <group>. Summarize AI backends and missing prerequisites without changing resources.

prompt_templates.title: Add a Model Backend
prompt_templates.prompt: Prepare commands and policies to add Azure OpenAI resource <resource> to APIM <name>. Use managed identity and least-privilege RBAC.

prompt_templates.title: Apply Governance Controls
prompt_templates.prompt: Design an inbound APIM policy for <workload> with token limits, semantic caching, content safety, rate limiting, and token metrics. Explain policy order.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Resilient Multi-Tenant Gateway
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a multi-region, multi-tenant AI gateway for <requirements>. Include authenticated tenant keys, backend failover, cost controls, observability, and a verification plan.

output_examples.input: Configure cost controls for a shared Azure OpenAI gateway.
output: Recommended controls: per-subscription token limits, semantic caching for non-streaming requests, and token metrics for chargeback.
Authentication: managed identity with Cognitive Services User scoped to each backend resource.
Validation: test quota responses, cache behavior, metric dimensions, and backend authorization before production.

output_examples.input: Troubleshoot repeated 401 responses from an Azure OpenAI backend.
output_examples.output: The review checks APIM managed identity status, scoped RBAC assignments, the Cognitive Services token audience, propagation delays, and backend identifiers.

best_practices: Use managed identities and narrow Azure RBAC scopes for all production backends.
Validate resource names, subscriptions, regions, and policy availability before running commands.
Use authenticated identities for rate-limit keys and keep credentials out of prompts, logs, and command output.
anti_patterns: Do not use DefaultAzureCredential in production Azure workloads.
Do not import mutable remote specifications without pinning and reviewing their contents.
Do not trust caller-supplied headers for tenant isolation or rate limiting.

faq.question: Does this skill deploy Azure API Management?
faq.answer: No. It configures and troubleshoots an existing APIM instance and directs deployment tasks to the azure-prepare skill.

faq.question: Which AI backends are covered?
faq.answer: The examples cover Azure OpenAI and Azure AI Foundry endpoints configured as APIM backends.

faq.question: Does it support MCP tools?
faq.answer: Yes. It explains API import, MCP exposure, content safety, and rate limiting for tool endpoints.

faq.question: Can these examples be used in production?
faq.answer: Review every placeholder, policy availability, RBAC scope, secret-handling step, and regional dependency before production use.

faq.question: How does the skill authenticate to Azure services?
faq.answer: It recommends managed identity for production and DefaultAzureCredential only for local development.

faq.question: Which assistant tools are supported?
faq.answer: The report declares compatibility with Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.
